articles.text: Editor: Having a son who was a Marine taught me many lessons. One is that the men and women who prepare for and serve on the front lines are rarely surprised when things don’t go as planned – and that this is often not the case higher up the command chain. The withdrawal from Afghanistan is a particularly devastating example. Our son has many friends who served there. None of them are stunned by the speed with which the Taliban retook the country nor by how quickly the evacuation process descended into chaos. Something is very wrong when high level military and government officials expected it to take 18 months for Kabul to fall and mere days to safely transport tens of thousands of U.S. citizens and Afghan allies out, but the soldiers who had actually been there knew otherwise. Or that it made sense to believe the Taliban would wield their newly regained power in a reasonable manner. Last Thursday evening we had a long talk with our son about the situation in Kabul and the buddy there he was waiting to hear from – a sweet kid from Wisconsin who called me “ma’am” and whose good humor kept the platoon going during even the most grueling field exercises. We asked what needs to change so this sort of catastrophe doesn’t happen again. “The people at the top have to talk to the guys with boots on the ground. Realize that sometimes a 19 year old grunt may know more than you do.” Seems pretty simple. Friday morning our son texted to say his friend is safe. His unit is being transferred out of Kabul because of all the casualties they took. –Kathleen Winters
articles.title: Lessons from Kabul

articles.text: It is important that the biblical story of Jonah, best known for the recalcitrant prophet spending three days and three nights in the belly of a great fish, be more than the beginning of a “did that really happen?’ debate. In fact, Jonah’s placement among the prophetic books of the Bible should tell us that, like the other prophetic works, the story of Jonah will cause us to consider our place in God’s world and confront us with critical questions about the way we are living our lives. When God’s word comes to Jonah instructing him to go to Nineveh, the capital city of Assyria, his first response is to flee in the opposite direction. Instead of joining a caravan heading east, he goes to the seaport of Joppa and buys a ticket to Tarshish, a city at the western edge of his Mediterranean world. He heads towards modern Spain instead of modern Iraq. Hebrew prophet that he was, Jonah would have been familiar with the poetry of Psalm 139 – “Where can I flee from your Spirit?” Still he gets on the ship heading to the edge of the known world. Here we encounter the first critical question of Jonah. Is there any place we can flee from God’s presence? Once at sea the ship encounters a violent storm. There is confusion and debate about what is happening and how to respond, but in rather short order Jonah says to the crew of the ship “Throw me overboard. I am the problem. Once I hit the water the seas will calm.” To their credit the sailors are not anxious to follow Jonah’s instruction and they try to row back to shore. It is only after this effort fails that they relent and hurl Jonah into the sea. At this point the “sea stops its raging” and the crew worships Jonah’s god. We are met with critical question No. 2. In the raging storm that is life in 2021 what is it that we need to throw overboard? Are there actions, beliefs, or attitudes that are not serving us well? articles.text: – Susan Miller-Davis former board president of Piedmont Connect The Piedmont City Council unanimously supported the Energy Innovation and Carbon Dividend Act (H.R. 2307), with all five council members endorsing it this summer. The bill was introduced in Congress on April 1 and imposes a fee on the carbon content of fuels, including crude oil, natural gas, and coal. These and other products derived from their fuels emit greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. The fee would be imposed on the producers or importers of the fuels, with the rate beginning at $15 per metric ton of CO2-e in 2021, increases by $10 each year, and is subject to further adjustments based on the progress in meeting specified emissions reduction targets. The bill is cosponsored by many Democratic representatives, including Rep. Barbara Lee and Rep. Jackie Speier from the Bay Area. “The act proposes an economy-wide ‘price on carbon’ to reduce carbon emissions quickly and at-scale,” former board president of Piedmont Connect (2019-2021), Susan Miller-Davis explained. The Piedmont resident also co-led Grasstops Engagement with the Alameda County chapter of Citizen’s Climate Lobby, one of nearly 600 chapters across the country working on carbon pricing. Citizens’ Climate Lobby is a not-for-profit, volunteer-driven organization which advocates for bipartisan climate change solutions in the United States Congress. “Piedmonters can feel proud that our local leaders are lending their voices toward addressing the climate crisis with urgency and at scale. I hope local business leaders, civic figures and residents will join the chorus now as climate policy is being hashed out in Congress,” said Miller-Davis. “A strong, economy-wide price on carbon could reduce America’s carbon pollution by 50% by 2030, putting us on track to reach net zero by 2050. It is one of the few solutions that addresses many sectors of the economy.” Piedmont has already taken aggressive action in battling climate change, including goals set in the Climate Action Plan, which set an ambitious goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) by 40% below 2005 levels by 2030, and as much as 80% below those levels by 2050. Miller-Davis acknowledged that measures taken by individuals, and small communities like Piedmont, are important and add up. She added, though, that top-down, economy-wide change is necessary to reduce emissions rapidly. enaugh described the importance of the bill’s passage. “We are all feeling the effects of carbon pollution everyday through natural disasters such as devastating wildfires, hurricanes, floods, and droughts, which were previously once in a lifetime occurrences but have now become annual events. There’s no denying the impact on all of us but certainly those with the fewest resources pay the highest price,” Cavenaugh said. “The Energy Innovation and Carbon Dividend Act is an important step toward necessary and bold climate action.” “As a small city, Piedmont can have an outsized influence on climate change when we use our voices to partner on regional and national efforts that will have the greatest impact. Individuals, businesses and local communities need to continue to do our part, but programs of this scale require urgent action by Congress to effectuate meaningful change on a national scale,” she said. City Council member Conna McCarthy added that, “supporting a price on carbon is one of several actions elected leaders can take to reduce the amount of carbon dioxide trapping heat on our planet. Putting a price on carbon pollution through a carbon tax encourages the transition to cleaner energy.” To find out more about how carbon pricing works and prospects for national legislation, join Piedmont Connect for a panel discussion and question-and-answer portion on carbon pricing, hosted by the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWVP), on Wednesday, September 22 at 4pm. The event is free online via Zoom and live-streamed on LWVP YouTube channel, but registration is required on the League’s website at lwvpiedmont.org/events. articles.text: Piedmont hosted a virtual community meeting on August 26 with researchers from the University of Texas at San Antonio who are analyzing Piedmont Police Department (PPD) calls for service data to examine how its services are used and prioritized. The city will use the analyses to inform future discussions of call responses. The University is focusing its research on the type of calls for service which officers respond to and the frequency of biasedbased calls for police intervention. The city stated that the work is “part of the effort to understand bias and the historical role racism has played in Piedmont and the community-at-large, in order to better lead a city which is a safe, welcoming, and equitable place for all people committed to by the City Council in Resolution 60-2020.” The proposal for research was approved by City Council on July 19. “Some of the most meaningful work we are engaged in as a city is an examination of what we do and how we do it, with an antibias and anti-racist lens. Police work in particular has appropriately been in the national, regional, and local spotlight in the wake of the killing of George Floyd,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said in introducing the community meeting. The purpose of the meeting was to describe and take questions on the upcoming analysis of police call data. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers spearheaded the initiative earlier this spring, Lillevand said, in a commitment to transparency and best practices in the PPD. The University of Texas, San Antonio’s (UTSA) Dr. Michael Smith and Dr. Rob Tillyer are leading the data analysis research. The bill was introduced in Congress on April 1 and imposes a fee on the carbon content of fuels, including crude oil, natural gas, and coal. These and other products derived from their fuels emit greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. The fee would be imposed on the producers or importers of the fuels, with the rate beginning at $15 per metric ton of CO2-e in 2021, increases by $10 each year, and is subject to further adjustments based on the progress in meeting specified emissions reduction targets. The bill is cosponsored by many Democratic representatives, including Rep. Barbara Lee and Rep. Jackie Speier from the Bay Area. “The act proposes an economy-wide ‘price on carbon’ to reduce carbon emissions quickly and at-scale,” former board president of Piedmont Connect (2019-2021), Susan Miller-Davis explained. The Piedmont resident also co-led Grasstops Engagement with the Alameda County chapter of Citizen’s Climate Lobby, one of nearly 600 chapters across the country working on carbon pricing. Citizens’ Climate Lobby is a not-for-profit, volunteer-driven organization which advocates for bipartisan climate change solutions in the United States Congress. “Piedmonters can feel proud that our local leaders are lending their voices toward addressing the climate crisis with urgency and at scale. I hope local business leaders, civic figures and residents will join the chorus now as climate policy is being hashed out in Congress,” said Miller-Davis. “A strong, economy-wide price on carbon could reduce America’s carbon pollution by 50% by 2030, putting us on track to reach net zero by 2050. It is one of the few solutions that addresses many sectors of the economy.” Piedmont has already taken aggressive action in battling climate change, including goals set in the Climate Action Plan, which set an ambitious goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) by 40% below 2005 levels by 2030, and as much as 80% below those levels by 2050. Miller-Davis acknowledged that measures taken by individuals, and small communities like Piedmont, are important and add up. She added, though, that top-down, economy-wide change is necessary to reduce emissions rapidly. enaugh described the importance of the bill’s passage. “We are all feeling the effects of carbon pollution everyday through natural disasters such as devastating wildfires, hurricanes, floods, and droughts, which were previously once in a lifetime occurrences but have now become annual events. There’s no denying the impact on all of us but certainly those with the fewest resources pay the highest price,” Cavenaugh said. “The Energy Innovation and Carbon Dividend Act is an important step toward necessary and bold climate action.” “As a small city, Piedmont can have an outsized influence on climate change when we use our voices to partner on regional and national efforts that will have the greatest impact. Individuals, businesses and local communities need to continue to do our part, but programs of this scale require urgent action by Congress to effectuate meaningful change on a national scale,” she said. City Council member Conna McCarthy added that, “supporting a price on carbon is one of several actions elected leaders can take to reduce the amount of carbon dioxide trapping heat on our planet. Putting a price on carbon pollution through a carbon tax encourages the transition to cleaner energy.” To find out more about how carbon pricing works and prospects for national legislation, join Piedmont Connect for a panel discussion and question-and-answer portion on carbon pricing, hosted by the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWVP), on Wednesday, September 22 at 4pm. The event is free online via Zoom and live-streamed on LWVP YouTube channel, but registration is required on the League’s website at lwvpiedmont.org/events. articles.text: The City of Piedmont and its housing consultant have announced three important community-outreach events this fall that ask for residents’ input on fair housing. At a May 3 meeting, City Council approved a proposal from Lisa Wise Consulting to prepare updates to the city’s Housing Element. The state is requiring that Piedmont create 587 new housing units by the end of the next Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) cycle in 2031. For more information, visit the city’s fair housing website, www.PiedmontisHome.org. Residents are encouraged to participate in the following events: • September 29 Joint meeting and study session of the Planning Commission and Housing Advisory Committee about the basic requirements for Housing Element updates in California and how fair housing makes Piedmont a great place to live. • October 21 Community meeting for new housing programs, including draft ADU (Accessory Dwelling Unit) and JADU (Junior Accessory Dwelling Unit) pre-approved plans and incentives, as well as draft objective design and development standards for multi-family housing development in Piedmont. • December 2 Community meeting to start the 2031 Housing Element Update.

A third strike team returned to action on a Type I fire engine on August 16 near Janesville, by Honey Lake, 70 miles north of Reno. The crew included Lt. Justin McNulty, Engineer Justin Morris, and firefighters Brian Gidney and Robb Hendry. Photo courtesy of the Piedmont Fire Department A giant fire header above the town of Taylorsville, with the Taylorsville Tavern on the right. Photo courtesy of the Piedmont Fire Department Seen on the left is the claw of a bulldozer used by a local resident to help clear away logs and fire fuel in Taylorsville. “[We were] immediately requested for structure protection in Janesville, so we fought fire from 10:00 p.m. to 3 a.m. That was literally going house to house trying to knock the fire down,” McNulty explained. The Piedmont crew joined up with the Inyo Hot Shots Crew who had been fighting the flames for two continuous weeks. That first intense five-hour stint was the start of a 38-hour shift for the Piedmont firefighters. Most shifts in a fire station are 24 hours, and McNulty said that 24-hour shifts are less disruptive to his sleep cycle than a 12-hour shift. In Janesville McNulty got creative and utilized some local help in the middle of the night using his flashlight to get the attention of a local man on a bulldozer in a field. “I told him we needed him to quickly circle these houses before we lose them. We were putting the fire out, but the fire load was tremendous, there were logs and fire fuel all over the fields next to the houses. It was awesome to see him push all that stuff out of the way,” McNulty recalled. He splashed posters with daily sales across the large plate-glass windows, and the customers flocked in. The Cognacq-Jaÿ couple was fully devoted to their burgeoning retail enterprise, and without children to raise, they worked every waking hour to innovate and elevate the department store model. They didn’t hesitate to copy from the “greats,” and copying Le Bon Marché, they remodeled extensively starting with plateglass to show off the fashions and flood the main floor in natural light. In the 1870s, it was revolutionary to mark the merchandise clearly with prices, and it freed shoppers to not have to ask. They were the first to invite customers to try on clothes before purchase. At a time when employers demanded 14 or even 16-hour days Monday through Saturday, La Samaritaine employees worked 10-hour days and half day on Saturday. Such a progressively lenient policy drew hordes of applicants. But they were strict too, particularly, Mme Jaÿ who demanded highly productive and attentive employees, or else a tardy worker might be terminated on the spot. Their motto was “On trouve tout à La Samaritaine,” meaning “One can find everything at La Samaritaine,” and inside the four locations, the merchandise ranged from girdles to lawnmowers. At the mark of 25 years in business, La Samaritaine broke a million francs in sales; and by 1925, the empire surpassed a billion francs in sales. By the late 1920s, their foundation was awash in funds. They had pioneered services such as a children’s nursery, a school, maternity clinic, and a nursing home, foremost for employees, and later opening to the public. articles.text: Photo by Todd Marshburn Piedmont will face Encinal for a scrimmage this Friday, September 3 at Witter Field after their initial scrimmage with Miramonte last week was canceled due to poor AQI. Piedmont’s varsity and JV football scrimmages with Miramonte last Friday evening were canceled due to poor air quality resulting from forest fires. The Air Quality Index in Orinda at game time was 150, above the acceptable standard. The Highlanders will host league opponent Encinal in a scrimmage game this Friday, September 3. With smoke entering the East Bay last Friday, August 27, Piedmont invited Miramonte to move the game to Witter, similar to offers by a number of schools in areas with cleaner air. By 3 p.m. that day, PHS football coach Jerome Johnson had not received confirmation of the game’s location, and canceled the trip to Orinda. “We made the attempt to move the scrimmage to Piedmont because, at a specific time, we had better air quality than Orinda and it’s just a short drive through the tunnel. We didn’t hear from then until 2:45, and the JV game was supposed to start at 4:30. I made the decision not to get our parents to go through the tunnel, and then have to turn around because Miramonte had poor air quality,” explained Johnson. But Piedmont had a bye (no game scheduled) for Week 1 of the North Coast Section calendar. Nearby Encinal had an opening this Friday as well, leading to the scheduled scrimmage on September 3. It is a critical time for Piedmont’s varsity team. Their small roster has been required to practice against Junior Varsity and haven’t sustained full-contact hits. “We need to get a scrimmage, because we haven’t had any action. We need to get ourselves some reps in a safe manner; we can’t go into a full game (the following week) without having any [game experience],” said Johnson. “We want to be put our kids in position to have success, and play safely to avoid injuries.” In a small step forward; the varsity has been able to add three players, and now has a roster of 20Since our last article on the football team, Johnson and company have added a few more players to bring their numbers up to 20 players. “Our numbers are low, but the kids are excited. We’re just excited to scrimmage and play again. We’re doing everything we can to have a season and doing all we can to protect our kids,” said Johnson. Encinal is in the same league with Piedmont in the Western Alameda County Conference’s newly created Mission division. Although it’s not typical for league opponents to offer clues to their plans, Encinal coach Keith Minor was also eager to get his squad some action after a sudden cancelation by Castlemont last Friday. “We do play Encinal in league, but their coach was very flexible because Castlemont canceled on them,” explained Johnson. “Coach Minor gave us a call and said, ‘Can we please get a scrimmage?, and I said, ‘Let’s make it happen.’” Piedmont will play Encinal this Friday at Witter Field. The JV scrimmage is at 4:30 p.m., followed by a varsity scrimmage at 7 p.m. Piedmont’s official season opens the following week, on Friday, September 10, also at Witter Field 7:00 p.m. in a game with Durham, a Div. 5 school south of Chico with an enrollment of 300. PHS offensive coordinator Jamar Julien, a former NFL running back, oversees drills with Batista Costa. Staff Photos

articles.text: Piedmont native Mackie McDonald climbed another notch on the ATP World Tour ladder of professional tennis players. Earlier on Tuesday, August 31, he upset No. 27 seeded David Goffin in straight sets, 6-2, 7-5, 6-3, in the first round of the prestigious U.S. Open. Goffin entered with a world ranking of No. 30. McDonald is No. 61. With the victory, he could surpass his career high ranking of No. 57. The U.S. Open first round has been a particular thorn in the side of McDonald. He’s been knocked out of the first round of the tournament three times – in 2016, 2018, and 2020. In each match, he won the first two sets, but lost in five. In 2016, McDonald lost to Chile’s Jan Satral, 4-6, 3-6, 6-3, 6-2, 6-2. Then in 2018, he fell in five sets to the Netherland’s Robin Haase, 4-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-1, 6-3. After his recovery from a leg injury in 2020, McDonald lost to No. 30 Casper Rudd in five sets, 4-6, 4-6, 6-4, 6-3, 6-2. This time, at age 26 and with a veteran mindset after recovering from a substantial torn hamstring tendon in 2019, McDonald is a man on a mission and perhaps entering the peak of his career. McDonald believes that the global pandemic enabled him to study his craft, build a further understanding of his body and how to stay healthy. “The start of 2020 was understanding my body,” McDonald said. “COVID actually gave me time to play tennis and get back to feeling like finding my game and stuff, because it takes time after an injury.” McDonald played up to his reputation against Goffin, gaining 14 aces, was successful on 71 percent of first serves, won five of 12 breakpoints, gained nine points at the net, and struck 50 winners. He’s finishing up a monumental month of August after jumping 43 positions when reaching the Finals at the Citi Open ATP 500 in Washington D.C. on August 8. Goffin is the sixth top-100 player on the ATP Tour that McDonald has defeated this month. At the Citi Open, Mackie handled Australia’s No. 80 Nick Kyrgios, 6-4, 6-4; France’s No. 50 Benoit Paire; Portugal’s No. 64 Ilya Ivashka, 6-4, 6-4; the U.S.’s No. 90 Denis Kudla, 6-3, 6-2; and Japan’s No. 56 Kei Nishikori in the semifinals to a three-set victory, 6-4, 6-3, 7-5. In 2019 at the time of his injury, McDonald watched his ranking dip from No. 57 to No. 132, and then to No. 272 due to a lengthy recovery. Now in the doorstep of a new career high, McDonald is set to face Keu Nishikori of Japan in the second round tomorrow, Thursday, September 2. The match streamed live on ESPN+. McDonald is currently ranked No. 61 in the world, four away from matching his career high.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Tahoe South A webcam photo of the Stateline area of South Lake Tahoe, which underwent an emergency evacuation on Monday. Monday’s big news was the emergency evacuation of South Lake Tahoe, a city of over 20,000. The Caldor Fire waging near South Lake Tahoe resulted in a hours-long traffic jam as residents funneled out on Highway 50. Cal Fire feared that dangerous winds could push the Caldor Fire toward the major tourist destination and town after the blaze breached Echo Summit. “Difficult road conditions, hard to access. It’s been burning in heavy timber, just very, very difficult conditions,” said Cal Fire chief Thom Porter. “We’ve been making headway at times. I reported last week about how we have effectively an inversion that puts kind of a lid on fire activity. But then when the air clears, it’s like taking a lid off of your pot of boiling water. All of a sudden, there’s that plume of heat and steam that comes out, same thing happens in a fire. It sucks in oxygen from all directions, and puts fires in all directions.” As of Tuesday night, August 31, the massive wildfire had grown 191,607 acres in 17 days and is only 16 percent contained. A total of 669 structures destroyed, and five people injured. More than 30,000 structures remain threatened with the blaze waging just a few miles from South Lake Tahoe. California governor Gavin Newsom declared a State of Emergency for Alpine, Amador, and Place Counties. “It is imperative that residents in the impacted areas stay safe and prepare to evacuate immediately if called for by local authorities,” Newsom said. “We thank all the heroic firefighters and first responders working around the clock to combat this rapidly spreading fire and to protect local communities across California this fire season.” The fire began on August 14, and high winds increased the size exponentially on August 16, jumping the Caldor Fire from 6,500 acres to 30,000 by August 17. On August 20, the fire had forced a closure on Highway 50, the main highway in and out of the south end of Lake Tahoe. Winds began driving the blaze toward the Lake Tahoe Basin one week later. Dixie Fire The Caldor Fire cannot be mentioned without acknowledging the huge Dixie Fire burning across five counties – Butte, Lassen, Plumas, Shasta, and Tehama. At 807,396 acres, it is the largest single source wildfire in California history and the second largest overall blaze behind last year’s August Complex Fire (1,032,000 acres). As of August 31, the Dixie Fire has been waging for 48 days and is at 48 percent containment. It has destroyed 1277 structures and damaged 92 others. The subsequent smoke has caused unhealthy air quality as far away as reaching as Utah and Colorado, according to the Associated Press. Both fires could result in poor air quality in the East Bay in September, resulting in the cancelling of some outdoor sports events. Of future concern is the history of hot, dry “Diablo” winds from inland areas typically pick up in September and October. articles.text: Piedmont’s volleyball team has opened its season with a win against St. Joseph in Alameda on August 24. One week later, Tuesday, August 31, it lost 3-1 to non-league opponent Skyline in Oakland. . “We’ve come a long way from last year because of COVID. This is the first regular season in two years,” said coach Leslie Blakely. “There are some things we’re doing well and some things we’re still missing. There’s a lot of progress, but there’s still a lot to work on to reach or full potential,” Volleyball has become the most popular girls’ sport in the fall season. According to Blakely, approximately 52 girls tried out for the team, resulting in the creation of a freshman team for the first time. “We had 52 girls tryout for the team. That’s huge. We hosted a lot of open gyms during the summer to build interest in the sport. When you see that many kids interested, you know the program is going to improve. Kids are interested and it’s our job to provide them with a place to play. It’s an exciting future for our girls’ team,” she said. The Highlanders will have a wealth of upperclassmen, including seniors Sophie Nevis, Ruby Shaffer, Ari Talwatte, Amelia Wire, Sofia Croley, Juniors Tara Kothari, Bree Deyoung, Shelby Cavenaugh, and Eden Lorin, while Sophomores Peterson Baur, Izzy Grimmer, and Sadie Town round out the lineup. “A lot of girls came back; they Tara Kothari had seven kills and an ace. Ruby Shaffer led Piedmont with 11 kills and two serving aces. are awesome. You can see the energy around the team they love to play,” said Blakely. Leading offensively for Piedmont against Skyline was Shaffer with 11 kills and Kothari with seven. Both are returning starters from last season’s team. In Tuesday’s match, Skyline won the first two sets 25-19 and 25-13 but the Highlanders rallied for a convincing 25-17 win in the third set. The Titans, however, prevailed in the fourth and final set, 25-19. In the first set, PHS trailed 7-0 but fought back to narrow the score to 22-19. Skyline reeled off three straight points to win on defensive errors by Piedmont. Similarly in the second set, Skyline opened to a 6-0 lead and did well to close 25-13. But Piedmont won the third set 25-18, starting off with a 10-5 lead until Skyline stormed back with five unanswered points. Then Piedmont reeled off four straight points, 14-10, then after a pair of Skyline points PHS went on another six-point scoring run, 20-12, closing out by allowing six more while scoring five. In the third set win, PHS had five aces—two by Nevis and Eden, and one by Kothari—and 11 kills; three by Shaffer and Kothari, two by Deyoung and Nevis, and one by Town. Piedmont finished with 11 aces on the night, including three for Nevis, two for Schaffer, two for Baur, two for Eden, and individuals for Town and Kothari. Offensively, Shaffer had 11 kills, Koathari had seven, Nevis had five, Deyoung had two, and Eden, Croley, Town, and Talwatte had one. Filled over by the reservoir is the former village of Crystal Springs, slightly northwest of the reservoir’s dam on Lower Crystal Springs. The small town was a resort area along a railroad, and was the last station and stagecoach location between San Mateo and Half Moon Bay. The Crystal Springs Hotel was built in the 1860s. Surrounded by farmland, it provided a luxurious stop for people going to San Francisco. In 1859, the San Mateo County Gazette called Crystal Springs “truly a proper resort. Staff Photo Known for the cycling popularity, San Mateo County closes a 2.5-mile segment of Canada Road to traffic on Bicycle Sundays. Photo courtesy of the San Mateo County Historical Association This is the only known depiction of the Crystal Springs Hotel. Staff Photo Lower and Upper Crystal Springs Reservoir are a popular cycling area. The history of the region dates back to the late 1800s. Situated in a little valley, thickly studded with the clustering live oaks, surrounded on every side by high mountains, shut out from cold winds, and rich in nature’s beauties, it is truly a proper resort for the lovers of pleasure,” wrote the Gazette, via Geocaching.com. However, the town’s success was short-lived and the land was purchased by the Spring Valley Water Company, which eventually became the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission. The town of Crystal Springs was filled over with water by 1887 when the dam was constructed. The Spring Valley Water Company was owned by William Bowers Bourn II, who spearheaded the merger between the San Francisco Gas and Electric Company and California Gas and Electric Company to create Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E). Surprisingly, there is no mention of William Bowers Bourn in PG&E’s history. At the end of the Upper Crystal Springs Reservoir is the Pulgas Water Temple which was created in part by Bourn and the SF Water Department in 1934 to commemorate the completion of the Hetch Hetchy Aqueduct. The Pulgas Water Temple is a collection of Corinthian style columns bearing the inscription: “I give waters in the wilderness and rivers in the desert, to give drink to my people,” Isaiah 43:20. Flowing water was originally visible from the well within the stone columns, but was covered in order to prevent trespassers from jumping into the canal. A half mile from the Pulgas Water Temple is the Filoli Historic House & Garden Estate in Woodside, Bourn’s 43-room mansion with 16 acres of gardens, on a 654-acre estate. Created in 1915, Bourn lived there during his final days in 1936. The exterior of the Filoli mansion was used in the 1981 television series, Dynasty. Tours are offered for $25. Should bikers or hikers park at the Canada Road Cycling Parking Area, it’s only a 2.2 trek to the Pulgas Water Temple. It is also just 2.2 miles to the Crystal Springs Dam from the parking area along CA-35. Parking at the Pulgas Water Temple is closed on weekends, but available to hikers and bikers. Staff Photo The Pulgas Water Temple was built in 1934 to commemorate the Hetch Hetchy Aqueduct providing drinking water to San Mateo County and San Francisco. Staff Photo A view inside the Pulgas Water Temple, where the well has been covered with a large metal grate to prevent thrill-seekers jumping into the canal. Photo courtesy of Filoli.org Near the Crystal Springs Reservoir is the Filoli House, both created by William Bowers Bourn II. His untold history lays the groundwork for the entire Crystal Springs Reservoir region.

articles.text: The UC Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) recently announced the return of in-person film screenings this month at the Barbro Osher Theater. The theater will also serve as the East Bay venue for the Mill Valley Film Festival in October. “It’s thrilling to welcome our community of filmgoers back to BAMPFA after this difficult year, and I can’t imagine a better way to do so than with a series of free screenings presented al fresco on the museum’s outdoor screen,” said Susan Oxtoby, BAMPFA’s director of film and senior film curator. “For nearly eighteen months, we’ve been deeply moved by the support of our devoted audiences, who have continued to engage with BAMPFA’s film programming during our pivot to virtual cinema. We’re delighted to invite our audiences to return in person now that restrictions have been lifted.” This month BAMPFA’s ongoing series “Documentary Voices” returns with a selection of both classic and contemporary films with historical value. The film today, September 1, is The Murder of Fred Hampton, a political documentary as Howard Alk investigates the killing of Black Panther and titular leader Fred Hampton. On Wednesday, September 15, is a documentary by Tatiana Huezo entitled Tempestad, with an introduction by Nicolas Pereda. The film is built around interviews with two women and uses cinematography to describe the presence of crime in Mexico. The film will be shown at 7 p.m. Berkeley Pacific Film Archive is located at 2155 Center Street in Berkeley. To obtain tickets, see: https://bampfa.org/program/documentary-voices. articles.text: Berkeley Botanical Garden at The University of California will host a Zoom program exploring the many species of butterflies that have taken residence in the gardens. The virtual butterfly walk will be held on Sunday, September 12, at 11 a.m. Join the gardens’ resident propagator Sal Levinson and garden volunteer Sarab Seth for an illustrated slideshow of butterflies found among the flowers this time of year. Those who tune-in will learn about the butterflies’ life cycle and host plants. articles.text: Photo by Cory Weaver Ailyn Perez was vocally compelling in the title role of San Francisco Opera’s production of Puccini’s Tosca. Opera review by Paul Hertelendy I dearly love this “shabby little shocker,” as the great Berkeley musicologist Joseph Kerman once termed it, surfeited as it is with melodrama. The opera Tosca embodies the most greed, real-world corruption, duplicity, betrayal, revolutionary activism, hypocrisy and sheer sexual desire of any of Puccini’s operas, all set in familiar sites of Rome, adding up to a stunning social critique of the composer’s homeland. It shows this very establishment composer as a political activist, protester and reformer for once. Naturally, no opera has ever had a greater hold on San Francisco, which staged it as the very first work in the War Memorial Opera House in 1932 and then in 41 different seasons since. What better work to reopen on-stage production after a galling 20-month pandemic shutdown? And what about the intriguing murder trial that would have followed, had Tosca not killed herself by jumping off a Rome parapet? Tosca was subjected to sexual submission to the evil Scarpia if she was to save her imprisoned lover/revolutionary. Instead, she grabbed a nearby dagger and dispatched Scarpia in her supreme act of public service. Murder? Manslaughter? Justifiable homicide? Good case study for law students, especially given Scarpia’s astute evidence-gathering to entrap both male revolutionaries on the lam. This ranks with a mere handful of other works, like Janacek’s The Makropulos Affair, as fodder for young attorneys or detectives. But as melodramatic opera, this one really works with its entirely American cast. The San Francisco Opera’s 2018 production propels it along with stirring leads as the lovers Tosca and Cavaradossi. In her first Tosca, Chicagoan Ailyn Perez was vocally compelling, with an upper octave stronger than the lower one. As the coquettish diva, she played the insecure jealousy card in act one very well, while also carrying out the most difficult pantomime of all as the tremulous murderer preparing a tomblike scene around the cadaver. Tenor Michael Fabbiano, who had never ventured Cavaradossi before this summer, was heroic and convincing as the maligned prisoner, bringing down the house with his solo of resignation “E lucevan le stelle” prior to the firing squad. Clearly, a major talent to watch and hear in the future. The love duets of the two were to melt over. Scarpia newcomer baritone Alfred Walker was still feeling his way into the role, both as actor and as singer with heft. Others of note: Soloman Howard as Angelotti; Dale Travis, the SFO’s most prevalent character bit player since Colin Harvey, as Sacristan; and my favorite hissthe-villain in all Puccini, Spoletta (Joel Sorensen), taking huge nightly tumbles courtesy of the irascible and imperious Scarpia. When heard August 27, this was a promising start for the new feminine SFO Music Director Eun Sun Kim and a great finale season for choral Director Ian Richardson if the robust church procession ending Act One was any indication. (He retires in December.) Director Shawna Lucey kept the movement going, literally; whenever things slowed, extras were hopping about on stage. Even her firing squad appeared made up of veteran troops. MUSIC NOTES – The San Francico Opera is authorized to sell out the whole house, if all are masked and vaccinated, because the entire cast itself is fully vaccinated, a company representative explained….Tosca runs through Sept. 5…. More future standing ovations at the S.F. Opera? If so, ascribe it in part to the new chairs installed all over during the long pandemic. The old ones, mostly allegedly from 1932, sank down, down, down, till you went out of sight far below, very often with unsettling squeaks as downward accompaniment... Jazz improvisers would create their own manner of phrasing, syncopation and melodic design, but they were influenced by what they heard in performances of classical music, marching bands and church music. Jazz was born in New Orleans in a mix of African, French and Spanish cultures. African Americans used European band instruments, the African banjo and marching drums to blend African rhythm with chromatics in the melody and with the harmonic darkening of European chords. As Wynton Marsalis said at Jazz At Lincoln Center on January 12, 2018, “The amalgam of elements in Afro-American music and in jazz come from different forms of European music, like the march form and the combination of a fiddle style or a European parlor piano style, which, when combined with the arpeggiated sound of a banjo and syncopation, becomes ragtime.” Chromatics were used by these eastern Europeans classical composers: Chopin (Polish) - Waltz in C# minor (1847); Tchaikovsky (Russian) - Lenski’s Aria (1879); Fučík (Czech) - Entrance of the Gladiators (1897), Thunder and Blazes (1901); Rimsky-Korsakov (Russian) - Flight of the Bumblebee (1900) Classical music, in the common practice period from 1600 to 1900. primarily used triads (three-note chords). articles.text: Baby Driver is a solid summer movie that is indeed more than the sum of its parts. You might be asking yourself, why would I spend almost two hours watching a film titled Baby Driver? The answer depends on why you watch movies and what you expect to take away from the story. As it turns out, audiences happen to have a nifty spectrum of films to choose from. But know that this movie is an off-the-wall adrenalin rush that is surprisingly original, despite its staccato-like tropes. It’s dark and amazing and, in a word, cool. Downright cool. Set in today’s Atlanta, it borders on being a spikey fable with characters that are created out of whole cloth, absent any backstory. They’re just there, bank robbers all, and every one of them is crazily compelling. There’s Baby (Ansel Elgort), a baby-faced young twenty-something who works for Doc (Kevin Spacey) and his revolving crew of bank heist sociopaths. Baby wears full-time ear buds (bad tinnitus), shades, and is a gifted getaway driver who handles a car like a Le Mans speedway artist. Ansel Elgort stars in Baby Driver. Of course, the cops give chase (more than once), but Baby is a stone cold wheelman who zigs when they zag, hurtling through urban traffic and never changes his I-pod mix. Pure genius. After each job the ensemble meets to divvy up the loot and that’s when the tattooed alumni from a local prison get to do their trash talking. It’s just great. The lead psychopath, Bats (Jamie Fox), a certifiable head case for which there is no rehab, does a running, demented patois that conveys with each sentence that he is always on the verge of dropping off a mental cliff and shooting somebody. Anybody. As Bats, he is well named. The only character with even a hint of backstory is Baby, raised by a wheelchair-bound foster dad who is deaf and can’t speak. Where did that come from? There’s a lot more, to include a great performance by Jon Hamm as seemingly sane Buddy and his amazing girlfriend, Darling, superbly played by Eliza Gonzalez. Just your average wigged-out bank job couple and really fun to spend time with. I’ll stop here and just assume that if you watch Baby Driver, you’ll want to experience all the fast and slow reveals without too much warning. So, enjoy. Baby Driver. Directed by Edgar Wright. Starring Ansel Elgort, Jamie Fox, Jon Hamm, and Eliza Gonzalez. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated R. Ansel Elgort, Jamie Fox, Eliza Gonzalez, and Jon Hamm in Baby Driver.

articles.text: Dustin Hoffman and Emma Thompson star in Last Chance Harvey. Last Chance Harvey uses a familiar template that Hollywood has often turned to, sometimes with great success: estranged father attends daughter’s wedding and after a series of unexpected events, some comedic, some dramatic, he finds redemption. What makes Harvey entertaining is not the story, but the fine performances of Dustin Hoffman and Emma Thompson. They are both charming and delightful to watch and raise this film to a new level by the sheer volume of their acting ability. Their meeting in a London bar is pure serendipity, and yet when they begin their hesitant, quasi-hostile dance of getting acquainted, they are so engaging it’s impossible not to conclude that this is a film that possesses a nice glow. At the outset, using deft parallel editing, we are introduced to Harvey Shine and Kate Walker and discover that they are both lonely people. Harvey has lost his job and seemingly his daughter, and Kate is convinced that she is defined by her age and seeming isolation. Without realizing it, they set out to prove the other wrong – about so many things. Watching them interact, first as strangers and then as friends, is to observe two consummate actors who can look into the camera and with a look, a smile, a raise of the eyebrows say volumes, making it hard to bid these two likable people adieu as the credits begin to roll. Last Chance Harvey. Starring Dustin Hoffman, Emma Thompson, James Brolin and Kathy Baker. Directed by Joel Hopkins. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: A scene from Disney’s Planes: Fire & Rescue. Planes: Fire & Rescue is a nice fit for kids 8-years-old and below, and is an ideal follow up to Disney’s animated Planes. Both star Dusty Crophopper (Dane Cook). It was in Planes that Dusty realizes his dream of becoming a world-class, hotdogging air-racer, and an international celebrity, basking in the continual attention of the cameras. But then, unexpectedly, as Planes: Fire Rescue begins, Dusty discovers that his gearbox is failing, the parts he needs to fix it aren’t available, so he can’t reach those top speeds that allow him to win races. And there is the problem that his much loved hometown airport, Propwash Junction, needs a serious updating. Its equipment is failing to meet compliance. But the situation gives Dusty something to do, which he is yearning to do. He decides to become an aerial firefighter, gets certified by the crusty, cranky Blade Ranger (Ed Harris) who is in charge of training for the Piston Peak squadron. And so begins the story of planes (Dusty now included) zooming through fire ravaged canyons, up into billowing clouds of smoke, swooping down to scoop up water from lakes and rivers, some dropping pink fire retardant. All of them are flying by the seat of their ailerons, the Piston Peakers risking their lives, so to speak, to protect those on the ground, which includes the ATV smoke jumpers, a courageous bunch who drop out of airplanes, parachute to the ground, and fight the raging fires. The hotshot crew of Piston Peak also includes military transport Cabbie (Dale Dye), and Lil’ Dipper (Julie Bowen), who has a crush on Dusty. And there’s May Day (Hal Holbrook), a dated fire and rescue truck, plus Windlifter (Wes Studi), whose helicopter blades are painted like feathers. One of the squadron’s missions turns out to be an allhands-on-deck attempt to save the Grand Fusel Lodge, its guests are all manner of transportation that fill the lobby/hanger and the rooms. Dusty, of course, must overcome his fear as he confronts the ultimate villain in the story, the unforgiving forest fires, such as those barreling down on the lodge. There’s lots of action, and Dusty manages to get out of some tight spots, as does the Piston Peak squadron. Sure, there is peril, but parents shouldn’t be concerned. articles.text: The Iron Giant, directed by Brad Bird, is based on the children’s book, written by Ted Hughes, published in 1968, and set in the U.K. in the late 60s. For the film, however, Bird chose to move it to Rockwell, a small 1950s downhome town in Maine. The story begins one night during a frightening storm when a huge comet streaks across the sky, and lands in the ocean off the Maine coast. The next night, a 9-year-old boy named Hogart (Eli Marienthal), a latchkey kid raised by his single mom Annie (Jennifer Aniston), leaves home to wander in the woods. His mom is working late at a local diner. To his surprise he discovers what caused the comet. It was a massive, metal-eating giant robot (Vin Diesel), some 50 feet tall, (similar to the giant bot, Gort, in the film The Day the Earth Stood Still), and looks like an erector set toy. The bot is about to eat a local electric substation, but Hogart, seeing the danger of the giant being electrocuted, switches off the power. And thus begins a friendship between the robot and the boy (who has dreamed of having a pet). In one early scene, while the robot is eating some railroad tracks, it collides with an oncoming train, causing it to derail. As a result of that incident, two things happen: Hogart discovers that the robot can self-repair, and a government agent, Kent Mansley (Christopher McDonald), arrives to investigate the accident. He’s suspicious, a bit paranoid, and is convinced there is an E.T-like threat to the town (perhaps the entire country). He is determined to track down whatever it is. articles.text: Here are the Best Wines of 2021 • I was so glad to get the email that the Family Winemakers of California had scheduled a tasting for San Francisco last weekend. It has been a year and a half since I last attended a live wine tasting in person, and this is one of my favorite wine events of the year. Many of the people pouring the wine have the same name on their name-tags as the name on the wine label. There is a warmth, and yes, love for the wines that you do not find at the more “corporate” type wine events. The span of different grape varietals was intriguing. Like to taste a Semillon or a Barbera? How about Barbara or Primitivo? Come on in, they’re all here. I admit that I was never really able to find out exactly what constitutes a “family winemaker.” The vast majority of the wineries seemed to span the spectrum from small mom and pop operations to small/medium size operations producing fewer than 10,000 cases per year. I took an experienced wine colleague with me to the event and we focused on small wineries with which we were unfamiliar. There were so many great wines at the tasting – literally hundreds. The following list catalogues the wines that stood out among a huge sea of also-rans. They are wines of great character and quality and are worth searching out. They show that some of the finest wines in California are created in small, unknown, out of the way places by wineries that are fueled by family love and devotion. 2016 Peterson Mendo Blendo Tollini Vineyard (Best Value) This value priced (under $20) blend of Syrah, Petite Sirah, Carignane and Grenache from Mendocino County is a delicious bargain. In the mouth it is bursting with blueberry, cherry and blackberry fruit with touches of earth and leather. It has just the perfect touch of oak that is intriguing but not overpowering. I would crack this open next time you hit the grill with some BBQ ribs. www. petersonwinery.com • 2018 Noria Pinot Noir Michael Valentine Vineyard This lovely Pinot Noir hails from the famed Russian River Valley, the home of some of California’s greatest Pinots. The wine has an exotic nose of cherries, herbs, and toast with a palate of raspberry, vanilla and licorice flavors with bright acidity and medium body. Perfect with grilled salmon. www.noriawines. com • 2016 Howell Mountain Vineyards Cabernet Sauvignon Beatty Ranch Super-intense rich and powerful, this dense purple wine offers up notes of beef, cassis, blackberry, licorice and earth. Full-bodied and incredibly balanced, this is wine for 25-30 or more years of aging. This takes no back seat to even the finest Bordeaux. www.howellmounta- • 2018 Nove Grenache It is fun to discover wonderful wineries I had never heard of. Nove, which hails from Lake County. They have put together a beautiful example of one of my favorite grapes. In much of the world Grenache is used as a blending grape, so it’s nice to see it bottled by itself. This version is medium bodied (half-way between Pinot Noir and Cabernet), and fruity with strawberry and cherry flavors with a hint of dust or earth. It is smooth and soft on the finish with no sharp tannins. www.novevineyards. com invineyards.com The 2016 Peterson Mendo Blendo from the Tollini Vineyard was the best value at under $20. • 2016 RISK Cabernet Sauvignon This Cab comes from a vineyard in Oakville in Napa Valley and is crafted by Lodi-based Cabana Wines. Dense, yet supple, with gorgeous blackberry, and plum notes revealing layers of sage and spice. Harmonious, with fine tannins adding grip as the fruit sails on to a long finish. Perfect partner to a grilled rib eye steak. • Silkwoood N/V Alicante Bouchet For most wine drinkers the name Modesto brings to mind giant quantities of cheap, rather ordinary wine. Not enough people know about Silkwood, Modesto’s producer of some of the state’s finest Syrahs and Petite Sirahs. Not only that, talented winemaker and owner John Monnich also bottles one of the finest Alicante Bouchet’s I have tasted. Once one of California’s most widely planted grapes, Alicante Bouchet has largely disappeared, which is too bad. This bottle shows the grape’s potential. It is inky dark and rich with deep plum and blueberry flavors. Layered and intense yet with a smooth satisfying finish. Worth searching out. www.silkwoodwines.com or wines.com

The Bay Area is defined by a myriad of water, bordered by the powerful Pacific Ocean, various rivers, reservoirs, lakes, and ponds. Even on the hottest days, though, it’s uncommon to find people swimming in these waters. Unlike Southern California, known for its sunny, warm beaches, Northern California is characterized by rocky, windswept, and often unforgiving waters. But groups of Bay Area-residents have been gathering at social clubs along the Bay for decades. Perhaps the most familiar of these is The Dolphin Club, a volunteer-led community of 1,675 members at Aquatic Park in San Francisco. It was founded in 1877 with 25 charter members with a commitment to spending more time in and on the Bay, which “continues to inspire today’s Dolphins.” Its members swim year-round in the Cove at Aquatic Park within a line of buoys parallel to the shore that marks a quarter-mile course. Public access to the club is slated to resume soon, and members can currently bring in two guests. Piedmont resident Josh Bernstein, a longtime open water swimmer, invited me to join a morning “social swim” on August 13, a day that started at 6 a.m. The temperature of the water was about 62 degrees Fahrenheit, considerably warm for the Bay, I was told. Still, the temperature in the city hovered just below 60 degrees at 7:30 a.m., the designated start-time for that morning’s swim. The Dolphin Club and other major social clubs along the bay closed for a period of time during the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, during which time members had to dress and prepare for swims in parking lots. Now that clubs are open, patrons are able to change into their wetsuits and swimsuits and take a much-welcomed hot shower indoors after their swim. I was advised to rent a full wetsuit, which can be done at a Sports Basement store conveniently located in San Francisco’s Presidio. Water temperatures can drop to 50 degrees in the winter, making a wet suit a necessity for most. It is highly recommended for novice open-water swimmers like myself. The synthetic rubber material known as neoprene is a popular choice among wetsuit manufacturers for both its flexibility and buoyancy. While it is possible to drown in a wetsuit, I was assured by Bernstein that it would be “very difficult to sink in one.” It is important to find one that fits snuggly with no air pockets that could potentially allow water in. It turns out that the biggest challenge of the morning was getting the wetsuit on properly. It can take some time, but tying plastic bags to my feet and hands allowed the neoprene to slide over and made the fitting process much easier. Preparing to swim in the cold Bay waters requires the right gear, and, of course, strong swimming skills. The swimmers are under no supervision of a lifeguard. According to the San Francisco Police Department Marine Unit, there have been several close calls in the Golden Gate National Recreation Area (GGNRA) this past year, primarily due to rip currents. San Francisco open shorelines do not have traditional lifeguards, but GGNRA provides Ocean Rescue personnel who patrol Ocean Beach with the primary mission of informing visitors about ocean risks. Swimming and wading at beaches are “strongly discouraged.” At Aquatic Cove, swimmers often swim in pods, and look out for one another. “Swimming in cold water is not for everyone,” Bernstein admitted. “There are significant factors - the cold, the current, and the waves. It takes time to become acclimated. When you start the sport, you don’t want to stay in for long. You could become hypothermic and lose the ability to exercise judgement.” Lesser dangers include the sea life. Sea lions are very territorial. Bernstein recalled a time when a fellow swimmer was bitten by a sea lion and was seriously injured, requiring a trip to the hospital. Despite these risks, proper research and preparation – and a trusted pod of skilled swimmers by your side – makes for an exciting and daring recreational activity. Wading in the Bay waters at daybreak and watching a fiery sunrise illuminate Ghirardelli Square and the San Francisco skyline – all before a full day at the office – is a truly indescribable experience. Open-water swimming in the Bay Area is by no means a new phenomenon but it would be inaccurate to claim it as a favorite pastime among Northern Californians. In fact, many swimmers were driven to the Bay by a combination of pool closures and pandemic restlessness, as evidenced by a slew of anecdotal reporting from SF Weekly, the Daily Cal, and other publications. Bernstein, a member of the Dolphin Club who now swims about five mornings a week, acknowledged that he has spent more time in the Bay because of pool closures. “Swimmers, like runners, are addicted to the sport,” Bernstein said. “When the pools closed, we were desperate to find water.” Bernstein said he started visiting the swim clubs more frequently during the pandemic despite their closures, and met other swimmers getting ready in the parking lots - mostly members of the Dolphin Club and its next door neighbor, the South End Rowing Club. He began linking up with a group that frequented the cove in the mornings for social swims like the one I visited. Similar to my first cold-water excursion on August 13, he recalled that the pod of swimmers were “very welcoming, and just invited me to go along with them.” Dr. Josh Bernstein happily moves through the cool water at Aquatic Cove in San Francisco.

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Ratatouille ingredients are in season and abundant at our markets. Now is the perfect time when ratatouille ingredients are abundant at our markets. Every year, late summer into early fall, versions of zucchini, eggplant, and tomato dishes appear on our table for breakfast, lunch and dinner. We enjoy ratatouille as a versatile accompaniment to eggs, sandwiches, pasta, and any grilled or roasted meats, poultry, or fish. Served at room temperature, this is ideal for a Labor Day picnic or barbeque. This presentation is showy, with the bright skins of the vegetables on full display as it’s arranged with the slices stacked on their edges. It’s easily adaptable to a variety of vegetables, so mix-and-match as suits your taste. Ideally prepared early in the day, this dish requires at least one hour in the oven and tastes best cooked and cooled. Better yet, make a day ahead and store in the refrigerator to let the flavors develop even further. Oven-Roasted Ratatouille Adapted from David Tanis, Saveur Magazine 2016 Makes about 3 – 4 cups, depending on the size of the vegetables Ingredients • 3 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, plus additional for the pan and drizzling atop • 1 large white onion, thinly sliced • 1 teaspoon fresh thyme, chopped • 1 teaspoon fresh marjoram, chopped • 4 cloves garlic, minced • 1/4 teaspoon crushed chile flakes, to taste • 3/4 pound zucchini, about 4 medium, cut into 1/4-inch coins • 3/4 pound firm eggplant, about 1 small, cut into 1/4-inch slices • 3/4 pound ripe tomatoes, about 3 medium, cored and cut into • • 1/4-inch slices Fresh basil leaves, to garnish Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste Instructions Lightly oil bottom and sides of a 2-quart baking dish, preferably ceramic. Using a 10-inch skillet/fry pan, place 3 tablespoons of olive oil and spread to evenly coat the bottom of the pan. Add the sliced onions with salt and pepper to taste. Cook until onions are softened and translucent, then add thyme, marjoram, and garlic. Continue cooking a few minutes until garlic softens but doesn’t begin to brown. Transfer to the prepared baking dish, spreading evenly, and set aside. Meanwhile position an oven rack to the lower third of the oven and preheat to 400° F. Atop the onion layer, arrange the zucchini, eggplant, and tomatoes in alternating rows with sliced vegetables stacked vertically on edge and slightly overlapping. You want to see the colorful skins on each row for the visual impact of the finished dish. Pack the rows together tightly and continue until the dish is filled. Season the vegetables with additional salt and pepper to taste and drizzle another tablespoon or so of olive oil. Bake for 15 minutes, uncovered, then reduce the heat to 350° F and bake until the vegetables are tender, about 45 – 60 minutes. Baking time will depend on how tightly the vegetables are packed. The vegetables will continue cooking with carry-over heat from the baking dish. Remove the dish from the oven and cool to room temperature. This allows for the flavors to develop further. Garnish with a flourish of fresh torn basil. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.

articles.text: After meeting for 15 months online, the First Mondays Reading Group finally convened in person on August 2 outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. On a lovely, mild day, the Park’s many trees provided an idyllic setting for the discussion. Twelve readers were on hand for a discussion of the August selection, The Fire Next Time by James Baldwin a national bestseller when it was published in 1963, and now considered a classic of American literature. The book’s title comes from a couplet in “Mary Don’t You Weep,” an African-American spiritual, with the verse, “God gave Noah the rainbow sign. No more water, the fire next time.” voice, and the power of his writing. They acknowledged that the book was timely but were sad to realize it was written nearly 60 years ago. The readers believe that our country has made progress with race relations, but it has been slow and uneven. There have been times when our nation has been struck hard, as we have been recently, by the fact that racial injustice and white supremacy beliefs are still widely present. Our country has responded to this realization in the past but it has often fallen back. The readers expressed hope that our country is now widely more fully aware of this. We are now being presented with tragic events, hard facts, and new social norms in the media and elsewhere, and the hope is that this will change how we see race and how our nation will conduct itself. As always, the greatest hope seems to be with young people for a more just future. The readers recognized the influence of Baldwin’s writing on contemporary writers that continues to the present. In July 2015, Ta-Nehisi Coates wrote an article to his nephew called “Letter to My Son” as a modern version of Baldwin’s letter, and he later published Between the World and Me that speaks about the current state of the Black experience in America. The readers also felt it is important to understand the context of the times when Baldwin was writing. It was the 1960s during a time of segregation and the civil rights movement was emerging with great social unrest. Baldwin wanted his white audience to better understand Black Americans’ struggle for equal rights. A number of writers had written of the injustices African-Americans experience, but Baldwin’s book was a clarion call The book is composed of two essays: “My Dungeon Shook: Letter to my Nephew on the One Hundredth Anniversary of the Emancipation” and “Down at the Cross: Letter from a Region of My Mind.” The first essay, written as a letter to Baldwin’s fourteen-year-old nephew, discusses the central role of race in American history. The second essay deals with the relations between race and religion, focusing on Baldwin’s experiences with the Christian church as a youth, as well as the Islamic ideas of Black Muslims in Harlem at that time. Many readers had not previously read his works, and appreciated Baldwin’s eloquence, his The Fire Next Time, by James Baldwin. for change in America in the 60’s. He warned that there would be “a fire next time” if there wasn’t change. The question for the readers was how many more fires our country will have to experience before we get his message. With the book conversations complete, it was time to discuss future books to read. The group had previously selected, Deacon King Kong by James McBride for September, and Nomadland by Jessica Bruder for October. Albert Chen told the group of Land Of Big Numbers by Te-Ping Chen, who happens to be Albert’s cousin. The book has received strong critical reviews and the group selected it for their November read. The group’s next meeting will be on Monday, September 13, at 1:30 p.m., one week after the Labor Day holiday, and held outside the Japanese Tea House. New members are welcome and there is no fee to participate. Registration is required with the Piedmont Recreation Department at jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, September 1, 2021 Walking Piedmont Continued from page 22 The famous California architect Bernard Maybeck is credited with designing this 5-unit multi-family Piedmont building which seems to be a hybrid between stacked flats and attached bungalows. It responds well to the hilly site and fits in with the surrounding single-family detached homes. An unobtrusive multi-family Piedmont building, made up of 4 stacked flats, each with its own separate street entry. It has the same architectural massing as the neighboring homes. A small, unobtrusive backyard second unit. The “outdoor room” formed by the cottage, fencing and planting is a useful amenity to this award winning “Tiny House” of 285 square feet. and building plans spread over acres of land. What this means is that well thought out and designed multi-family buildings with neighborhood compatible massing, building heights, materials, architectural styles, and colors can be a visual enhancement that makes for a richer, more interesting city. One of the main urban design and architectural objections to different uses, types and sizes of buildings next to each other is the abruptness of change. This is especially true in residential areas, where people live. For example, think of a new seven-story glass clad office building located in a two story residential neighborhood – clearly not appropriate. But what about a 4-story mixed use building in a 2-3 story neighborhood? What about a well designed 3-story apartment? It’s often hard to say without seeing it in context. Each case is different because each site and its local surrounding context is different and has to be evaluated as such. It occurs to me that the principal issue with denser multi-family housing is most often not more people, but instead….more cars. Next: Multi-family Housing, Part 3: The Car Dilemma Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years.
